title: Draupadi's question
hookLine: a messenger comes to Draupadi's door, and she sends back a question: whom did you lose first?
carry: asking what dharma requires is dharma too

cards: The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly.
In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that; it's the thread of everything that follows.
So Duryodhana turns to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms.

teach.b: The usher tells Draupadi that Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come.

She sends him back with one thing to ask the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake.
She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher asks it in the hall.
Yudhishthira says nothing; the telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses. Duryodhana says: let her come and ask it herself.

Draupadi sends the usher again, this time with a question for everyone: ask the assembly what is right for me to do. The usher hesitates to go a third time, so Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana. Now the teaching.
In Hindu tradition, dharma isn't something you swallow in silence.
It is asked about, argued, and answered. The Upanishads are full of students questioning teachers; the Gita itself is Arjuna's questions to Krishna.

And Draupadi, staked and summoned, does the most dharmic thing in the hall: she asks what dharma is here, and makes the elders face it. Many Hindus still name her each morning in a short verse honoring five great women.
For today: when something is done to you, or in your name, asking respectfully on what grounds is not disrespect. It's dharma too.

how: Draupadi's question is retold in homes, dance and theater, and it's discussed by readers and commentators as a question about dharma and law that the epic leaves open.

o: whether a man who'd lost himself could still stake her
whether the dice used in the game were loaded
whether her husbands would take her into exile

games.q: the question carried — tap the pairs.
p: carried the question back and forth

s: in Hindu tradition, questioning elders about dharma is always disrespect
the Upanishads and the Gita are built on questions, and Draupadi asked the whole assembly what was right.
Yudhishthira answered her question at once
the telling says he sat silent and answered not a word.
he said she couldn't be a slave, since Yudhishthira staked her after losing himself.

games.q: in class, an aunty says 'don't question the elders' when Priya asks how Yudhishthira could stake Draupadi. what fits the story?
o: stay quiet; asking about dharma is rude.
ask respectfully: Draupadi asked the whole hall what was right, and the tradition honors her for it.
games.why: Draupadi sent her question to Yudhishthira and then to the assembly. Hindu tradition is full of questions about dharma, asked with respect.

practice: Bring to mind a question you've wanted to ask but haven't, about a decision made for you, or something that didn't add up. Shape it as plainly and respectfully as Draupadi did: who decided, and on what grounds?
If you pray, bring the question into your prayer and ask for the courage to say it kindly; if not, let it sit with you in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's question. Sent back with a messenger: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? Then sent to the whole hall: what is right?

orig.note: Sanskrit praśna: a question; also the name of the Prashna Upanishad, built on questions.

carryVoice: Your line: asking what dharma requires is dharma too. One plain question, and a whole hall has to face it. That's the week.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana sends Vidura, who refuses; the usher Pratikamin sent to Draupadi; her question whether Yudhishthira lost himself first; Yudhishthira's silence; the second message to the assembly; Duhshasana sent)

Questioning as part of dharma: student questions in the Upanishads; the Bhagavad Gita as Arjuna's questions to Krishna; Draupadi named among the five honored women (pancha-kanya) in a traditional morning verse
